explanation: It is an ocean in the making: Africa and Arabia are slowly pulling apart along a rift beneath it, so the sea is very gradually widening.

claims.text: The Red Sea separates the Arabian Peninsula from north-east Africa.
The Arabian Sea lies south-east of the Arabian Peninsula, and the Mediterranean lies north of Africa.
Africa and Arabia are pulling apart along a rift beneath the Red Sea, which is slowly widening.

evidence.restatement: The Red Sea lies between the Arabian Peninsula and Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea in north-east Africa.
The Arabian Sea lies south-east of the Arabian Peninsula, between it and India, and the Mediterranean lies along Africa's north coast.
The Red Sea fills a rift where the African and Arabian plates are moving apart, so it is slowly widening.

issues.note: Rival test: the Gulf of Aden, an arm of the Arabian Sea, lies between Yemen and Somalia, so a pedant could argue for the Arabian Sea. The Red Sea is the sea between the peninsula and Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea, so the key stands. No change needed.

evidence.restatement: The Red Sea separates north-east Africa (Egypt, Sudan, Eritrea) from the Arabian Peninsula (Saudi Arabia, Yemen).
The Arabian Sea lies east and south-east of the Arabian Peninsula, towards India; the Mediterranean lies north of Egypt and Libya.
The Red Sea fills a rift where the African and Arabian plates are moving apart, so it is slowly widening.

issues.note: 'North-east Africa' can be read to include the Horn of Africa, and the Gulf of Aden (counted as part of the Arabian Sea in some atlases) lies between Yemen and Somalia, so the Arabian Sea lure is not wrong in every reading. The Red Sea is still the only sea that separates Arabia from Egypt, Sudan and Eritrea, so one answer holds. Optional: name Egypt in the stem.
